new_statements.quote: del Barco notes that in his notes on Cochimí, "I left accents out because it is enough to tell the uninitiated that the accent [stress] is always on the last syllable" (Mixco 1978:105). The grave accents in other Cochimí data from the Jesuits mark this final stress, which serves to distinguish phonological words. However, sometimes a semantically close-knit phrase may be treated as a phonological word. ... Sometimes the final stress may spread to a preceding epenthetic vowel. [p. 6:] Phonological words/close-knit phrases are defined by a strong stress on the last syllable. Stress may spread an epenthetic vowel preceding a stressed syllable.
new_statements.citation: Shaul, David Leedom. 2020. Baja California Languages: Description and Linguistic Prehistory (Southern California Pacific Linguistics, Part 1). Survey of California and Other Indian Languages, Report 19. Berkeley: University of California.
new_statements.locator: Ch. 2 'The Sound Pattern of Cochimí', section 'Syllable Structure and Prosody', p. 10 (PDF p. 18); supporting statements p. 6 (PDF p. 14) and comparative table p. 50

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the final syllable of the phonological word (del Barco, the 18th-c. Jesuit describer, states the accent is always on the last syllable; Jesuit accent marks and Shaul's analysis of the texts agree); a close-knit phrase may behave as one phonological word with a single final stress; a consonant or vowel immediately before the stressed final syllable may lengthen.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; only that final stress 'may spread to a preceding epenthetic vowel'.
new_statements.exceptions: Close-knit phrases (e.g. noun + locative) may be treated as a single phonological word with one final stress; for the Gabb (San Borja) and Hervás varieties the records carry no stress marking, so Shaul lists them as '[probably final]' (p. 50); Gatschet 1877:388 says the final-stress tendency shows more in nouns than in verbs.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word, which can extend over a semantically close-knit phrase; evidence is philological (Jesuit orthographic accents c. 1740-1790 and del Barco's explicit remark, via Mixco 1978:105), not instrumental — the language is extinct.
new_statements.identity_note: Shaul 2020's 'Cochimí' chapter describes Jesuit Cochimí (del Barco's San Javier/Comondú-area texts plus Clavijero/Ducrue material), i.e. coch1272 proper; he treats Hervás Cochimí, Gabb Cochimí (San Borja, 1867) and Robinia (Bartlett MS) as separate varieties/languages — for Gabb and Hervás Cochimí no stress is recorded ('[probably final]'), Robinia shows final stress by acute accents. Glottolog files Nebé (Shaul 2023) under coch1272 as well; Robinia has no glottocode. Gatschet 1877's 'Oxytonirung ist die Regel' refers to Cochimí generally (Jesuit texts, Gabb, Robinia).

sources.citation: Gatschet, Albert S. 1877. Der Yuma-Sprachstamm nach den neuesten handschriftlichen Quellen dargestellt. Zeitschrift für Ethnologie 9: 341-350, 365-418.
sources.note: p. 366: 'im Yuma der Accent von der Wurzel nach der Endsilbe vorzudringen strebt... im Cochimi (nebst Waikuru) ist Oxytonirung sogar die Regel... Wo aber alle Worte, oder doch die grosse Mehrzahl oxytonirt sind, wie im Cochimi'; p. 387: Gabb's San Borja list is of 'dieses oxytonirten, stark consonantischen Idioms'; p. 388: Robinia's vocabulary in Spanish orthography has 'den Wortton zumeist auf der Endsilbe'; in Clavigero's four Cochimí Lord's Prayers 'zeigt sich die Tendenz, den Wortton auf die letzte Silbe zu verlegen', more in nouns than verbs.
Gives a tentative consonant/vowel chart citing Mixco 1978:13-19; nothing on stress.
